title: India and the U.S. Just Signed a Ten-Year Defence Framework. It Covers Everything From Javelins to Jets.
excerpt: Rajnath Singh and Pete Hegseth formalised the agreement on the sidelines of ADMM-Plus in Kuala Lumpur, calling it the beginning of a 'new chapter' in bilateral defence ties.
body:
India and the United States have signed a ten-year Defence Framework Agreement, the most comprehensive military pact between the two countries in at least a decade.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth formalised the agreement on the sidelines of the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) in Kuala Lumpur, with senior officials from both sides present. The framework establishes a long-term roadmap for military collaboration, capacity enhancement, and joint projects across the Indo-Pacific.

"We have held telephonic conversations thrice. I am delighted to be meeting you in person on the sidelines of ADMM-Plus," Singh said. "On this occasion, I feel a new chapter will begin today with the signing of the Defence Framework. I am confident that under your leadership, India-US relations will further strengthen."

## What the Framework Covers

The agreement goes well beyond symbolic partnership language. It lays out policy direction for what officials describe as "the entire spectrum" of the India-U.S. defence relationship — from joint military exercises and intelligence sharing to co-production of weapons systems and technology transfer.

Hegseth described the framework as "a defining moment" and outlined the shared strategic vision. "This 10-year US-India Defence Framework is ambitious. It's a significant step for our two militaries, a roadmap for deeper and even more meaningful collaboration ahead. It underscores America's long-term commitment to our shared security and our strong partnership," he said.

The defence relationship has deepened rapidly in recent years. India now operates a growing fleet of American-origin platforms: C-130J Super Hercules and C-17 Globemaster III transport aircraft, P-8I Poseidon maritime patrol planes, CH-47F Chinook heavy-lift helicopters, MH-60R Seahawk naval helicopters, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, M777 howitzers, Harpoon anti-ship missiles, and MQ-9B armed drones.

## Co-Production on the Table

Perhaps the most consequential element of the framework is the push toward domestic co-production. Both sides have committed to pursuing deals for manufacturing Javelin anti-tank guided missiles and Stryker infantry combat vehicles in India — a significant departure from the traditional buyer-seller relationship that has defined Indian defence procurement for decades.

The co-production agenda aligns with India's broader push to build a domestic defence industrial base. Defence Minister Singh released the Delegation of Financial Powers to Defence Services-2026 (DFPDS-2026) this month, granting the armed forces over ₹1.25 lakh crore in annual revenue procurement powers. Financial powers for indigenisation and research and development have been doubled.

"This Defence Framework will provide policy direction to the entire spectrum of the India-US Defence Relationship," Singh wrote on X after the meeting. "It is a signal of our growing strategic convergence and will herald a new decade of partnership."

## The Strategic Context

The signing comes at a moment of both opportunity and tension in the India-U.S. relationship. On the diplomatic track, Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to meet President Trump on the sidelines of the G7 summit in France next week, with trade, visas, and energy cooperation high on the agenda.

But the relationship has been strained by several recent developments. U.S. tariffs on Indian goods, the killing of three Indian sailors in a U.S. strike on a ship off Oman as part of the Iran blockade, and Trump's repeated claims about intervening in India's brief conflict with Pakistan last year have all created friction.

The defence framework appears designed to anchor the relationship in its strongest dimension — military cooperation — even as other areas face turbulence. Singh's Malaysia visit also included talks with Malaysian Defence Minister Khaled Nordin and participation in sessions focused on regional peace and counter-terrorism efforts.

India and Malaysia currently serve as co-chairs of the ADMM-Plus Experts' Working Group on Counter Terrorism for 2024-2027.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the deepening defence relationship has concrete implications. A stronger India-U.S. strategic alignment tends to correlate with a more favourable political environment for Indian-Americans on issues ranging from visa policy to bilateral trade. Defence co-production deals also create jobs and industrial partnerships that span both countries.

The framework also signals that despite the friction points in the broader relationship, the structural alignment between the world's two largest democracies continues to deepen. As one senior U.S. official put it: "Our strategic alignment is built on shared interests, on mutual trust, and commitment to a secure and prosperous Indo-Pacific region."

The next major test of this alignment will come at the G7 summit, where Modi and Trump will sit down to discuss trade, energy, and the fallout from the Iran war — issues where India's interests and America's actions have not always aligned.
